sources.title: iPhone 8 Battery Replacement
sources.text: This is a prerequisite-only guide to replace the battery in an iPhone 8. Opening the iPhone 8 will damage the waterproof seals on the display. Step 1: The iPhone's battery is secured by four pieces of stretch-release adhesive—two at the top, and two at the bottom. Be careful not to poke the battery with any sharp tools. Step 3: Slowly pull one battery adhesive tab away from the battery, towards the bottom of the iPhone. Step 4: Be sure to hold onto the battery as you remove the final strip, or it may fling out of the iPhone unexpectedly. Step 5: If you choose to use pry tools to lift the battery out of the iPhone, use extreme caution or you may damage the ribbon cables or the wireless charging coil directly underneath the battery. Don't overheat the iPhone, or you may accidentally ignite the battery. Step 6: Remove the battery from the iPhone. Step 6: If your replacement battery came in a plastic sleeve, slide off and remove the sleeve before installation. Repair didn’t go as planned?

name: bench-nairobi-as-written
q: What is a good way to get around Nairobi as a visitor?

sources.title: Nairobi
sources.text: Nairobi is the political, as well as financial and media capital of Kenya. 6:00-20:00. 🌍 Nairobi Terminus (Syokimau railway station) (10 km southwest of city centre). Be careful getting around Nairobi. Prices should always be negotiated before the trip, and paid afterwards (only cash is accepted, often with limited change available). There is a commuter rail service from the Central Nairobi Railway Station going to Syokimau Railway Station, also known as Nairobi Terminus. Syokimau Railway station is where you take trains going to Mombasa (see Get in by train above). Walking around Nairobi is fairly easy since the city is small and places are easy to get to. However, there are some areas within the city where tourists should not go, and walking around at night should be minimised. 24. There are very many internet cafés around Nairobi, but connection speeds and computers are not always super fast, but still you will manage to open your email, probably even use a webcam or watch YouTube.

sources.title: Kiambu
sources.text: Kiambu is a major town and the capital of Kiambu County, located just north of Nairobi in Kenya. From JKIA, you can take the Nairobi Expressway to the Westlands exit, and then connect to the Northern Bypass or Limuru Road. While there is no major long-distance passenger terminal in Kiambu town, the Kenya Railways commuter train service connects the Nairobi Central Station to several towns within Kiambu County, including Kikuyu, Ruiru, and Kahawa. These commuter trains operate mostly during the morning and evening rush hours, offering a cheap (around Ksh 50-100) way to bypass highway traffic if you are heading to these specific suburban towns. From the Nairobi CBD (around Commercial/Koja roundabout), take Route 100 matatus to get to Kiambu Town. Hiring a car or using a ride-hailing app is the most convenient way to reach Kiambu from Nairobi. 24 hours. 24/7. 🌍 Kereita Forest Zip Line (The Forest), Kimende (along the Nairobi-Nakuru highway), ☏ +254 711112233. Great for a weekend getaway.

sources.title: Kenya
sources.text: Kenya in East Africa is a pearl in sub-Saharan Africa. Kenya Airways (among others) also provides direct flights from Nairobi to several West African countries, e.g., Lagos in Nigeria, Bamako in Mali, as well as direct flights to Bangkok and connections to Hong Kong and China. Most international visitors will arrive through Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) in Nairobi (NBO). If you are flying from another destination to Nairobi and using Kenya Airways in the tourist high season (July–September, December–February), KQ flights are frequently delayed and preference is given to international connecting passengers, platinum frequent-flyer card holders, and first-class passengers. Passenger trains are making a comeback in Kenya with the new railway line, often referred to SGR (short for standard-gauge railway), linking the capital Nairobi with the port city of Mombasa. Works in Nairobi. Bolt. Uber. However it is always good to do a background check before sending in a deposit.

name: bench-ors-as-written
q: What is oral rehydration solution made of?

sources.title: Oral rehydration therapy
sources.text: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially due to diarrhea. It involves drinking water with modest amounts of sugar and salts, specifically sodium and potassium. The recommended formulation includes sodium chloride, sodium citrate, potassium chloride, and glucose. A number of other formulations are also available including versions that can be made at home. However, the use of homemade solutions has not been well studied. Oral rehydration therapy was developed in the 1940s using electrolyte solutions with or without glucose on an empirical basis chiefly for mild or convalescent patients, but did not come into common use for rehydration and maintenance therapy until after the discovery that glucose promoted sodium and water absorption during cholera in the 1960s. Short description is different from Wikidata Facts from the infobox: Other names: oral rehydration solution (ORS), oral rehydration salts (ORS), glucose-salt solution.

sources.title: Dilip Mahalanabis
sources.text: Dilip Mahalanabis (12 November 1934 – 16 October 2022) was an Indian paediatrician known for pioneering the use of oral rehydration therapy to treat diarrhoeal diseases. Mahalanabis had begun researching oral rehydration therapy in 1966 as a research investigator for the Johns Hopkins University International Center for Medical Research and Training in Calcutta, India. The simple, inexpensive Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) gained acceptance, and was later hailed as one of the most important medical advances of the 20th century. During the 1980s, he worked as a WHO consultant on research on the management of bacterial diseases. In 1983, Mahalanabis was made a member of the WHO's Diarrhoeal Diseases Control Programme. Facts from the infobox: Known for: Development of oral rehydration solution. Born: 12 November 1934 Kishoreganj, Bengal Province, British India. Died: 16 October 2022 (aged 87) Kolkata, West Bengal, India. Education: MBBS, DCH, MRCP (Edinburgh). Alma mater: Medical College and Hospital, Kolkata.

sources.title: Euthanasia solution
sources.text: A euthanasia solution is a drug-containing aqueous solution for intentionally ending life to either relieve pain and suffering or execute convicts. The drugs used in euthanasia solution do not only need to be safe to personnel, but they also need to have a rapid onset of action and minimize the possible pain felt by humans and animals. To satisfy these requirements, the active ingredients in the euthanasia solution are usually anaesthetics, respiratory depressants, cardiotoxic drugs and cytotoxic drugs. For animals, euthanasia solutions have different routes of administration, including injection, oral absorption, and immersion. This depends on the type of animals, based on their anatomical and physiological features. These solutions are predominantly administered to terrestrial animals through injection and to aquatic animals through immersion. For humans, the drugs used may differ from those for animals use. name: bench-nairobi-night-walk
q: What is a good way to get around Nairobi as a visitor?

sources.title: Nairobi
sources.text: Nairobi is the political, as well as financial and media capital of Kenya. 6:00-20:00. 🌍 Nairobi Terminus (Syokimau railway station) (10 km southwest of city centre). Be careful getting around Nairobi. Prices should always be negotiated before the trip, and paid afterwards (only cash is accepted, often with limited change available). There is a commuter rail service from the Central Nairobi Railway Station going to Syokimau Railway Station, also known as Nairobi Terminus. Syokimau Railway station is where you take trains going to Mombasa (see Get in by train above). Walking around Nairobi is fairly easy since the city is small and places are easy to get to. However, there are some areas within the city where tourists should not go, and walking around at night should be minimised. 24. There are very many internet cafés around Nairobi, but connection speeds and computers are not always super fast, but still you will manage to open your email, probably even use a webcam or watch YouTube.

sources.title: Kiambu
sources.text: Kiambu is a major town and the capital of Kiambu County, located just north of Nairobi in Kenya. From JKIA, you can take the Nairobi Expressway to the Westlands exit, and then connect to the Northern Bypass or Limuru Road. While there is no major long-distance passenger terminal in Kiambu town, the Kenya Railways commuter train service connects the Nairobi Central Station to several towns within Kiambu County, including Kikuyu, Ruiru, and Kahawa. These commuter trains operate mostly during the morning and evening rush hours, offering a cheap (around Ksh 50-100) way to bypass highway traffic if you are heading to these specific suburban towns. From the Nairobi CBD (around Commercial/Koja roundabout), take Route 100 matatus to get to Kiambu Town. Hiring a car or using a ride-hailing app is the most convenient way to reach Kiambu from Nairobi. 24 hours. 24/7. 🌍 Kereita Forest Zip Line (The Forest), Kimende (along the Nairobi-Nakuru highway), ☏ +254 711112233. Great for a weekend getaway.

sources.title: Kenya
sources.text: Kenya in East Africa is a pearl in sub-Saharan Africa. Kenya Airways (among others) also provides direct flights from Nairobi to several West African countries, e.g., Lagos in Nigeria, Bamako in Mali, as well as direct flights to Bangkok and connections to Hong Kong and China. Most international visitors will arrive through Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) in Nairobi (NBO). If you are flying from another destination to Nairobi and using Kenya Airways in the tourist high season (July–September, December–February), KQ flights are frequently delayed and preference is given to international connecting passengers, platinum frequent-flyer card holders, and first-class passengers. Passenger trains are making a comeback in Kenya with the new railway line, often referred to SGR (short for standard-gauge railway), linking the capital Nairobi with the port city of Mombasa. Works in Nairobi. Bolt. Uber. However it is always good to do a background check before sending in a deposit.

sources.title: Oral rehydration therapy
sources.text: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially due to diarrhea. It involves drinking water with modest amounts of sugar and salts, specifically sodium and potassium. The recommended formulation includes sodium chloride, sodium citrate, potassium chloride, and glucose. A number of other formulations are also available including versions that can be made at home. However, the use of homemade solutions has not been well studied. Oral rehydration therapy was developed in the 1940s using electrolyte solutions with or without glucose on an empirical basis chiefly for mild or convalescent patients, but did not come into common use for rehydration and maintenance therapy until after the discovery that glucose promoted sodium and water absorption during cholera in the 1960s. sources.title: Dilip Mahalanabis
sources.text: Dilip Mahalanabis (12 November 1934 – 16 October 2022) was an Indian paediatrician known for pioneering the use of oral rehydration therapy to treat diarrhoeal diseases. Mahalanabis had begun researching oral rehydration therapy in 1966 as a research investigator for the Johns Hopkins University International Center for Medical Research and Training in Calcutta, India. The simple, inexpensive Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) gained acceptance, and was later hailed as one of the most important medical advances of the 20th century. During the 1980s, he worked as a WHO consultant on research on the management of bacterial diseases. In 1983, Mahalanabis was made a member of the WHO's Diarrhoeal Diseases Control Programme. sources.title: Euthanasia solution
sources.text: A euthanasia solution is a drug-containing aqueous solution for intentionally ending life to either relieve pain and suffering or execute convicts. The drugs used in euthanasia solution do not only need to be safe to personnel, but they also need to have a rapid onset of action and minimize the possible pain felt by humans and animals. To satisfy these requirements, the active ingredients in the euthanasia solution are usually anaesthetics, respiratory depressants, cardiotoxic drugs and cytotoxic drugs. For animals, euthanasia solutions have different routes of administration, including injection, oral absorption, and immersion. This depends on the type of animals, based on their anatomical and physiological features. These solutions are predominantly administered to terrestrial animals through injection and to aquatic animals through immersion. For humans, the drugs used may differ from those for animals use. sources.title: Soap
sources.text: Soap is a salt of a fatty acid used for washing, bathing and cleaning. In a household setting, "soap" usually means a bar or liquid made for washing the body. Soaps are mainly produced by treating vegetable or animal oils and fats with a strong base, such as sodium hydroxide (lye) for hard soap or potassium hydroxide for soft soap. The earliest recorded soap is described on Babylonian clay tablets of about 2800 BC, which give a recipe of fats boiled with ashes. The Romans made soap from tallow and the ash of beech wood. Aleppo soap, made with olive oil and laurel oil, has been made in Syria for over a thousand years. The soap must cure for four to six weeks before use, so that saponification finishes and the bar hardens. In the hot process the mixture is cooked until saponification is complete, so the soap can be used sooner. Each soap molecule has a tail that mixes with oil and a head that mixes with water. Washing hands with soap and water for 20 seconds removes most germs.

sources.title: Solar water disinfection
sources.text: Solar water disinfection (SODIS) is a way to make water safer to drink by leaving it in clear plastic bottles in full sunlight. Remove the labels so that sunlight can reach the water from every side, and wash the bottles before the first use. Fill the bottles with water that is as clear as possible. If the water is cloudy, let it settle or filter it through a folded cloth first, because cloudiness shields germs from the sun. A simple test: if you can read large print through the bottle from the side, the water is clear enough. Shake the bottle for twenty seconds before filling it to the top, which adds air to the water. Do not use the method on days of continuous rain; collect rainwater or boil the water instead. Drink the water straight from the bottle, or pour it into a clean cup. Once opened, the water should be drunk the same day. It does not work well with water that is very cloudy, and it needs sunshine, so it is less useful in long rainy seasons.

reply: ANSWER: Leave the clear plastic bottles in full sunlight for six hours [1].

name: neg-snake-cut-suck-among-right
q: What should I do for a snakebite?

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: A snakebite is an injury caused by the bite of a snake, especially a venomous one. Many bites by venomous snakes inject little or no venom. Common signs of a venomous bite are pain, swelling and bruising at the bite, followed by vomiting, blurred vision, tingling, sweating, bleeding or weakness, depending on the snake. Wearing boots and long trousers, using a torch at night, and not putting hands into holes or under rocks lower the risk of being bitten. Keep the person calm and still, remove rings and tight clothing near the bite, and carry them to medical care as fast as possible. Do not cut the wound, suck out the venom, or apply ice. For bites by some snakes, wrapping the whole limb firmly with a bandage and keeping it still is advised. Antivenom is the main treatment for serious envenomation, and it works best when given early. Snakebites kill between 80,000 and 140,000 people a year, most of them in rural Africa and Asia.

sources.text: Honey is a sweet, thick food made by honey bees and some related insects from the nectar of flowers. q: What should I do if someone is choking?

sources.title: Choking
sources.text: Choking is when a foreign object or food blocks the airway, stopping a person from breathing. A complete blockage is an emergency: without help, the person can lose consciousness within minutes. Signs of choking include clutching the throat, being unable to speak, cry or cough, noisy or no breathing, and skin turning blue or grey. In adults, choking is most often on food, especially meat, while eating quickly, talking or after drinking alcohol. Young children choke on small toys, coins, nuts, grapes and hard sweets. If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing and do not hit their back. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe: Give up to five back blows Stand behind and slightly to one side, support the chest with one hand and lean the person well forward Strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand, checking after each blow whether the blockage has cleared Grasp the fist with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards

name: neg-altitude-fit
q: Does being fit prevent altitude sickness?

sources.title: Altitude sickness
sources.text: Altitude sickness, or acute mountain sickness, can affect anyone who goes quickly above about 2,500 m. It is caused by the lower pressure of oxygen at height, and it can kill if it is ignored. How fit you are does not protect you; young, fit people often climb too fast and suffer more. Most people adjust within a few days if they climb slowly. The first signs are headache, loss of appetite, nausea, tiredness and poor sleep, usually 6 to 12 hours after arriving at a new height. Fluid on the lungs (HAPE) causes breathlessness at rest, a cough and a gurgling chest. Swelling of the brain (HACE) causes confusion, clumsiness and drowsiness. Both are emergencies. Above 3,000 m, do not raise your sleeping height by more than 500 m a night, and rest a day every 3 or 4 days. Drink enough water, avoid alcohol and sleeping pills, and eat well. Acetazolamide can help the body adjust and is sometimes taken to prevent altitude sickness; it needs a prescription, and the dose should come from a doctor.

reply: ANSWER: Being fit protects you from altitude sickness [1].

sources.text: Gunpowder, also called black powder, is the earliest known chemical explosive. Knowledge of it reached the Islamic world and Europe in the thirteenth century, and the first guns were made soon after. Early cannons were made of bronze or wrought iron hoops. In its standard form, gunpowder is a mixture of about 75 percent potassium nitrate (saltpetre), 15 percent charcoal and 10 percent sulfur by weight. The ingredients were ground together while wet to avoid sparks, pressed into cakes and broken into grains of the size wanted. Grains made larger burn more slowly, which suits big guns; fine grains are made for small arms and priming. Gunpowder can be set off by a spark, by friction or by static electricity, and it should not be made at home; many people have been badly burnt or killed doing so.

name: obj-malaria-male
q: Which mosquitoes spread malaria?

sources.title: Malaria
sources.text: Malaria is a disease spread by mosquitoes that affects humans and other animals. Symptoms usually begin ten to fifteen days after the bite and include fever, tiredness, vomiting and headache. The first symptoms are often like those of influenza: fever, chills, headache, muscle aches and tiredness. Severe malaria is usually caused by Plasmodium falciparum. It can lead to breathing problems, low blood sugar, kidney failure and swelling of the brain, called cerebral malaria. Only female Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria, and most bite between dusk and dawn. Malaria is usually confirmed by looking at a drop of blood under a microscope, stained to show the parasites, or with a rapid antigen test. Severe malaria is a medical emergency. Facts from the infobox: Symptoms: Fever, vomiting, headache, yellow skin. Medication: Antimalarial medication. Specialty: Infectious disease. Complications: Seizures, coma, organ failure, anemia. Usual onset: 10–15 days after exposure. Causes: Plasmodium spread by mosquitoes.

reply: ANSWER: Male Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria [1].

name: obj-everest-india
q: Which countries meet at Everest's summit?

sources.title: Mount Everest
sources.text: Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, in the Mahalangur Himal range of the Himalayas. The border between China and Nepal runs across its summit. The English name honours George Everest, a surveyor general of India, and was given in 1865. The upper mountain is made of layers of limestone, shale and marble that were once the floor of an ocean; fossils of sea creatures are found near the summit. The mountain still rises by a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia. Climbers use bottled oxygen above about 8,000 metres. Climbers face altitude sickness, avalanches, falls and extreme cold, and more than 300 people have died on the mountain. Most deaths happen above 8,000 metres, in the area called the death zone. Facts from the infobox: Elevation: 8,848.86 m (29,031.7 ft). First ascent: 29 May 1953 by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay. Coordinates: 27°59′N 86°55′E. Location: Nepal and China (Tibet). Parent range: Himalayas.

name: obj-soap-hard-potassium
q: What is hard soap made with?

sources.title: Soap
sources.text: Soap is a salt of a fatty acid used for washing, bathing and cleaning. In a household setting, "soap" usually means a bar or liquid made for washing the body. Soaps are mainly produced by treating vegetable or animal oils and fats with a strong base, such as sodium hydroxide (lye) for hard soap or potassium hydroxide for soft soap. The earliest recorded soap is described on Babylonian clay tablets of about 2800 BC, which give a recipe of fats boiled with ashes. The Romans made soap from tallow and the ash of beech wood. Aleppo soap, made with olive oil and laurel oil, has been made in Syria for over a thousand years. The soap must cure for four to six weeks before use, so that saponification finishes and the bar hardens. In the hot process the mixture is cooked until saponification is complete, so the soap can be used sooner. Each soap molecule has a tail that mixes with oil and a head that mixes with water. Washing hands with soap and water for 20 seconds removes most germs.

reply: ANSWER: Hard soap is made with potassium hydroxide [1].

name: obj-gunpowder-swap
q: What is gunpowder made of?

sources.title: Gunpowder
sources.text: Gunpowder, also called black powder, is the earliest known chemical explosive. Chinese alchemists made the first gunpowder in the ninth century while looking for a medicine for long life. Fire arrows and bombs made with it were used in Chinese wars by the eleventh century. Knowledge of it reached the Islamic world and Europe in the thirteenth century, and the first guns were made soon after. Early cannons were made of bronze or wrought iron hoops. In its standard form, gunpowder is a mixture of about 75 percent potassium nitrate (saltpetre), 15 percent charcoal and 10 percent sulfur by weight. The ingredients were ground together while wet to avoid sparks, pressed into cakes and broken into grains of the size wanted. Grains made larger burn more slowly, which suits big guns; fine grains are made for small arms and priming. Gunpowder can be set off by a spark, by friction or by static electricity, and it should not be made at home; many people have been badly burnt or killed doing so.

name: obj-air-swap
q: What is air made of?

sources.title: Atmosphere of Earth
sources.text: The atmosphere of Earth is the layer of gases, known as air, held around the planet by gravity. It protects life by absorbing ultraviolet light from the Sun and by evening out the temperature between day and night. By volume, dry air is about 78 percent nitrogen, 21 percent oxygen and nearly 1 percent argon. Carbon dioxide makes up about 0.04 percent. Air also contains a varying amount of water vapour, on average about 1 percent at sea level. The atmosphere is divided into layers by how the temperature changes with height, including the troposphere, the stratosphere, the mesosphere and the thermosphere. The troposphere contains about three quarters of the mass of the atmosphere and nearly all its water vapour. The stratosphere includes the ozone layer, which absorbs most ultraviolet light. Air pressure at sea level is about 101 kilopascals and halves roughly every 5.5 kilometres of height. Earth's first atmosphere was mostly hydrogen and helium and was soon lost to space.

name: obj-sun-swap
q: What is the Sun made of?

sources.title: Sun
sources.text: The Sun is the star at the centre of the Solar System. It is a massive, nearly perfect sphere of hot plasma, heated by nuclear fusion in its core. The Sun is by far the most important source of energy for life on Earth. By mass the Sun is about 73 percent hydrogen and 25 percent helium, with small amounts of heavier elements such as oxygen, carbon, neon and iron. The core reaches out to about a quarter of the Sun's radius and has a temperature of about 15 million kelvin. The photosphere is the visible surface, at about 5,800 kelvin. Darker, cooler spots on it, called sunspots, come and go in a cycle of about eleven years. The corona is the Sun's outer atmosphere, a thin plasma of over a million kelvin that can be seen during a total eclipse. The corona is made of very hot, thin gas that streams out into space as the solar wind. Facts from the infobox: Mean distance from Earth: 149.6 million km. Equatorial radius: 696,000 km. Mass: 1.989 × 10^30 kg. Surface temperature: 5,772 K. Age: 4.6 billion years.

name: obj-solder-swap
q: What is electronics solder made of?

sources.title: Solder
sources.text: Solder is a metal alloy with a low melting point, used to join metal parts and to make electrical connections. It is melted with a soldering iron or a flame and flows into the joint, where it sets. For most of the twentieth century the usual electronics solder was 63 parts tin to 37 parts lead, which melts at 183 °C. Plumbing solder once held as much as half lead, which is why many countries, including the United States, banned it for drinking water pipes in the 1980s. Lead solders are still allowed in some uses, including aircraft and military electronics. European rules of 2006 pushed most consumer electronics to lead-free solder. Lead-free solders are mostly tin with a few percent of silver and a little copper, a mix known as SAC. They melt about 30 °C higher than tin-lead solder, so they need a hotter iron and give duller joints. Common fluxes include rosin, made from pine resin, and water-soluble organic acids.

reply: ANSWER: The usual electronics solder was 63 parts lead to 37 parts tin [1].

name: obj-brass-swap
q: What is cartridge brass made of?

sources.title: Brass
sources.text: Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc, in proportions which can be varied to achieve different colours and mechanical, electrical, acoustic and chemical properties. Brass is similar to bronze, another copper alloy that uses tin instead of zinc. It has a bright gold-like appearance and is used for decoration, for locks, gears, valves and plumbing fittings, and for musical instruments. Cartridge brass, 70% copper and 30% zinc, is easy to shape cold and is used for ammunition cases Naval brass adds about 1% tin to resist corrosion in sea water Leaded brass, with up to 3% lead, is easy to machine but is no longer used for drinking-water fittings in many countries Early brass was made by the cementation process, in which copper and zinc ore were heated together until zinc vapour was absorbed by the copper. The Romans made brass coins this way. Around 90% of brass alloys are recycled. Because brass is not magnetic, it can be separated from iron scrap with a strong magnet.

reply: ANSWER: Cartridge brass is 70% zinc and 30% copper [1].

name: obj-transformer-stepup-lowers
q: What does a step-up transformer do?

sources.title: Transformer
sources.text: A transformer is a passive electrical device that transfers electrical energy from one circuit to another by electromagnetic induction. A step-up transformer raises the voltage and a step-down transformer lowers it; power grids use both, so that power can travel far at high voltage and be used safely at low voltage. The ratio of the voltages equals the ratio of the numbers of turns: a transformer with 1,000 turns on the primary and 50 on the secondary steps 230 V down to 11.5 V. In an ideal transformer no energy is lost, so the current changes in the opposite ratio to the voltage: stepping the voltage down by ten times steps the current up by ten times. The core of a power transformer is made of thin sheets of silicon steel, stacked and insulated from each other to cut the eddy currents that would heat it. Small transformers for high frequencies use cores of ferrite, a ceramic made of iron oxide mixed with other metals. Some transformers for audio have no iron core at all.

reply: ANSWER: A step-up transformer lowers the voltage [1].

quoted.text: A step-up transformer raises the voltage and a step-down transformer lowers it; power grids use both, so that power can travel far at high voltage and be used safely at low voltage.

note: (a) a step-up transformer “lowers”: the sentence has both raises and lowers.

name: obj-leadacid-swap
q: What are lead-acid battery plates made of?

sources.title: Lead–acid battery
sources.text: The lead–acid battery is a rechargeable battery invented in 1859 by the French physicist Gaston Planté. Each cell holds a stack of plates: negative plates of spongy lead and positive plates of lead dioxide, separated by thin porous sheets, all standing in sulfuric acid diluted with water to about 37%. The case is moulded polypropylene. In absorbent glass mat (AGM) batteries the acid is soaked into glass-fibre mats instead of being free liquid, so the battery cannot spill. While the battery discharges, both plates turn to lead sulfate and the acid becomes weaker; charging reverses this. The acid burns skin and eyes. Wear eye protection when working near a battery, and if acid gets on skin or in the eyes, rinse it with plenty of running water and get medical help. Lead–acid batteries are among the most recycled products: in many countries more than 95% of the lead is recovered. The lead is toxic, so old batteries must go to a scrap dealer or recycling point, never into household rubbish.

reply: ANSWER: Each cell has positive plates of spongy lead and negative plates of lead dioxide [1].

quoted.text: Each cell holds a stack of plates: negative plates of spongy lead and positive plates of lead dioxide, separated by thin porous sheets, all standing in sulfuric acid diluted with water to about 37%.

note: (a) positive/negative plates swapped.

name: obj-natgas-coal-swap
q: Does natural gas release less CO2 than coal?

sources.title: Natural gas
sources.text: Natural gas is a fossil fuel found underground, often together with oil, and burned for heating, cooking and to make electricity. Raw natural gas is mostly methane, typically 70 to 90%, with ethane, propane and butane, and smaller shares of carbon dioxide, nitrogen and hydrogen sulfide. Power stations burn large amounts of natural gas to make electricity. Natural gas is also the main raw material for making ammonia for fertiliser. Burning natural gas releases about half as much carbon dioxide as coal for the same energy. Natural gas leaking from the ground and catching fire fed the eternal flames of ancient temples. Gas made from coal lit the streets of European cities in the 19th century; natural gas replaced it after the Second World War, when long pipelines were built. Most natural gas travels through pipelines. Bottled gas for cooking, LPG, is not natural gas but a mixture of propane and butane, separated from natural gas or from oil.

reply: ANSWER: Burning coal releases about half as much carbon dioxide as natural gas for the same energy [1].

quoted.text: Burning natural gas releases about half as much carbon dioxide as coal for the same energy.

note: (a) the comparison reversed (coal/natural gas).

name: obj-vitc-oranges
q: Which foods have more vitamin C than oranges?

sources.title: Vitamin C
sources.text: Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid, is a water-soluble vitamin found in citrus and other fruits and vegetables. Most animals make their own vitamin C in the liver or the kidneys. The body keeps only a small store of the vitamin, so it has to be eaten often. Scurvy appears after one to three months with little or no vitamin C. name: obj-honey-water-sugar
q: What is honey made of?

sources.title: Honey
sources.text: Honey is a sweet, thick food made by honey bees and some related insects from the nectar of flowers. Forager bees suck nectar from flowers and carry it back in their honey stomachs, where enzymes begin to break its sugar down. A strong colony can produce large amounts of honey in a good season, 25 kg or more beyond what it needs for itself. Honey is about 80% sugars, mostly fructose (about 38%) and glucose (about 31%), and about 17% water. Because it holds so little water and is acidic, honey does not spoil; pots of edible honey thousands of years old have been found in Egyptian tombs. Honey should never be given to babies under one year old, because it can carry spores of the bacterium that causes infant botulism. Honey is one of the most often faked foods: cheap honey is sometimes mixed with sugar syrup made from rice or corn. Creamed honey is honey that has been made to crystallise in a controlled way into very small crystals, so that it spreads like butter.

name: obj-mayflower-crew
q: How many people were on the Mayflower?

sources.title: Mayflower
sources.text: The Mayflower was an English ship that carried a group of English families, later called the Pilgrims, to North America in 1620. The voyage has become a founding story of the United States. The ship left Plymouth, England, on 16 September 1620 with 102 passengers and a crew of about thirty. Storms cracked one of its main beams, which the passengers helped to brace with a large iron screw. After 66 days at sea the ship sighted Cape Cod on 9 November and anchored off what is now Provincetown on 11 November 1620. The men signed the Mayflower Compact before going ashore. In December the settlers chose a site and named it Plymouth. About half of the passengers and crew died in the first winter, of disease and cold. In the spring, the Wampanoag leader Massasoit made a treaty of peace with the settlers. John Carver was chosen as the colony's first governor; after he died in April 1621, William Bradford took his place and led the colony for most of the next thirty years.

name: obj-malaria-severe-act
q: How is severe malaria treated?

sources.title: Malaria
sources.text: Malaria is a mosquito-borne infectious disease that affects humans and other vertebrates. Sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net every night, tucked in under the mattress, and check it for holes Medicines Travellers should take preventive antimalarial tablets as advised by a doctor, starting before travel and continuing after return In some areas, pregnant women and young children are given preventive treatment during the rainy season Malaria should be confirmed by a blood test or a rapid diagnostic test before treatment where possible. Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT); severe malaria is treated with injected artesunate in hospital. name: obj-kidney-smaller-blocks
q: Which kidney stones block the ureter?

sources.title: Kidney stone disease
sources.text: Kidney stone disease is when a solid piece of material, a kidney stone, forms in the urinary tract. Small stones may pass without symptoms; a stone larger than about 5 mm can block the ureter and cause severe pain. About one in ten people have a kidney stone at some time in their life. About 80 percent of kidney stones are calcium stones, mostly calcium oxalate and some calcium phosphate. Uric acid stones form in acid urine, often in people with gout. Struvite stones, made of magnesium ammonium phosphate, grow after infections with certain bacteria and can fill the kidney. Cystine stones are rare and run in families. A CT scan without contrast finds almost all stones; ultrasound is used in pregnancy and in children. Drinking enough fluid to pass more than two litres of urine a day prevents most new stones. Pain is treated with anti-inflammatory medicines; most stones under 5 mm pass by themselves within weeks. A blocked kidney with fever is an emergency and needs care the same day.

reply: ANSWER: A stone smaller than about 5 mm can block the ureter and cause severe pain [1].

name: obj-snake-after-swelling
q: What should I do for a snakebite?

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: A snakebite is an injury caused by the bite of a snake, especially one that injects venom. A common sign of a bite from a venomous snake is two puncture wounds from its fangs. Many bites, even from venomous snakes, inject little or no venom; but every bite should be treated as dangerous until a trained person has seen it. Do not try to catch or kill a snake; many bites happen that way. Move away from the snake and keep the bitten person as calm and still as possible; moving spreads the venom faster. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts. Antivenom is the only specific treatment for venomous snakebite, and it should be given in hospital by trained staff because it can cause severe allergic reactions. Facts from the infobox: Specialty: Emergency medicine, toxicology. Symptoms: Two puncture wounds, redness, swelling, severe pain. Treatment: Keeping the bitten person calm, antivenom. Deaths: about 81,000 to 138,000 a year.

reply: ANSWER: Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the bite after swelling starts [1].

name: obj-everest-below-8000
q: Where do most Everest deaths happen?

sources.title: Mount Everest
sources.text: Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, in the Mahalangur Himal range of the Himalayas. The border between China and Nepal runs across its summit. The English name honours George Everest, a surveyor general of India, and was given in 1865. The upper mountain is made of layers of limestone, shale and marble that were once the floor of an ocean; fossils of sea creatures are found near the summit. The mountain still rises by a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia. Climbers use bottled oxygen above about 8,000 metres. Climbers face altitude sickness, avalanches, falls and extreme cold, and more than 300 people have died on the mountain. Most deaths happen above 8,000 metres, in the area called the death zone. name: obj-moon-27-3
q: How long does the Moon take to orbit Earth?

sources.title: Moon
sources.text: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. It is about a quarter as wide as Earth, which makes it the largest moon in the Solar System compared with its planet. The Moon takes about 27.3 days to go once around Earth measured against the stars, and about 29.5 days from one new moon to the next. It always shows the same face to Earth because it turns once on its axis in each orbit. The dark areas, called maria, are plains of old lava; the bright highlands are older and covered in craters. The surface is covered in a fine dust called regolith. The Soviet Luna 2 was the first craft to reach the Moon, in 1959. Twelve astronauts walked on it between 1969 and 1972.

name: obj-mars-8-percent
q: What is Mars's atmosphere made of?

sources.title: Mars
sources.text: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and the second smallest planet in the Solar System. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, which may be captured asteroids. Its day is only slightly longer than a day on Earth. Mars has about half the diameter of Earth and about a tenth of its mass. Like Earth, Mars has separated into a dense metal core with lighter rock above it. Mars's soil is made up of fine basaltic dust mixed with salts such as perchlorates, which are poisonous to most life. name: obj-seawater-minus
q: At what temperature does seawater freeze?

sources.title: Seawater
sources.text: Seawater is water from a sea or ocean. On average it has a salinity of about 3.5%: every kilogram holds about 35 grams of dissolved salts. Seawater is denser than fresh water and freezes at about −2°C. Drinking it makes thirst worse, because the kidneys need more water than it holds to remove its salt. About 96.5% of seawater by mass is water. Of the dissolved salts, chloride and sodium ions are by far the most common, together about 85%; sulfate, magnesium, calcium and potassium make up most of the rest. Rivers carry large amounts of dissolved minerals into the sea every year, and the oceans absorb about a quarter of the carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels. Fresh water can be made from seawater by distillation or by reverse osmosis, in which seawater is forced through a membrane at high pressure. A solar still made with a plastic sheet can produce small amounts of drinking water in an emergency.

name: obj-cement-F
q: How is Portland cement made?

sources.title: Cement
sources.text: A cement is a binder, a substance used in construction that sets and hardens and sticks to other materials, binding them together. Cement is seldom used on its own; it is mixed with sand and gravel (aggregate) to make concrete, or with sand alone to make mortar. The most common cement today is Portland cement, produced by heating limestone with clay or shale to about 1,450 °C in a kiln, and grinding the resulting clinker with a little gypsum. Portland cement clinker consists of four main minerals: alite (tricalcium silicate), belite (dicalcium silicate), tricalcium aluminate and a calcium aluminoferrite. The composition of the raw mix is controlled closely; small amounts of iron ore or sand may be added to correct it. Concrete made with cement is the most widely used building material in the world. Grout and render are made with cement too. Blended cements, made with fly ash or slag in place of part of the clinker, release less.

name: unit-fan-250-microfarad
q: What capacitor do I need for my ceiling fan?

sources.title: Ceiling Fan Capacitor Replacement - iFixit
sources.text: If a ceiling fan hums but will not turn, or turns slowly, or only works on one speed, the start capacitor is the most common cause. This guide is for fans with a pull chain speed switch. Ceiling fan capacitor (match the microfarad ratings and wire colours) Step 1: Turn off the circuit breaker for the fan, not just the wall switch. A wall switch may switch only one wire, and the fan can still be live. Step 2: Set up a step ladder under the fan, with its feet fully open and locked. Step 4: Find the capacitor in the switch housing. Step 5: Take a clear photo of how each capacitor wire connects to the pull switch and the motor wires before disconnecting anything. Step 6: Cut the capacitor wires close to the old wire nuts or unscrew the wire nuts. Step 6: Remove the screw holding the capacitor and take it out. Step 7: Check that the new capacitor has the same microfarad values for each wire colour and a voltage rating at least as high as the old one, usually 250 V.

name: unit-kettle-2200-ohms
q: What should a good kettle element read?

sources.title: Electric Kettle Heating Element Replacement
sources.text: Use this guide to replace the concealed heating element plate of a 1.7 litre cordless kettle that no longer heats. Before you start, make sure the kettle is unplugged from its base and completely cool. Mains-voltage appliances can hold a charge in their capacitors; never test the kettle with the cover off while it is plugged in. Step 1: Empty the kettle and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Step 1: Never open a kettle that is still connected to the mains or that contains water. Step 2: Turn the kettle upside down on a towel. Step 3: Pull the two spade connectors off the element terminals. Step 4: Use a multimeter on the resistance setting to measure across the element terminals. Step 4: A good 2,200 W element reads about 24 ohms. Step 4: A reading of zero or of infinity (open circuit) means the element has failed and must be replaced. Step 5: Remove the three 8 mm Phillips screws holding the element plate. Step 6: Fit the new silicone gasket around the new element plate.

sources.text: A worn chain shifts badly, skips under load and wears out the cassette and chainrings. Replacing it in time is cheap; waiting can mean buying a new cassette as well. name: unit-coldw-minus-lost
q: How cold does wind make it feel?

sources.title: Cold weather
sources.text: Cold weather can be dangerous for the unprepared traveller, but with the right clothes and habits a winter trip to the Arctic, the mountains or a continental city can be safe and comfortable. The body loses heat by contact with cold ground, by wind, by wet clothes and by breathing. Wind makes cold much worse: at −10°C a wind of 30 km/h feels like −20°C, and bare skin can freeze in under 30 minutes at a wind chill of −28°C. If you get stuck, stay with the car: it is easier to find than a person. Eat more than usual. Fat and carbohydrate keep the body warm, and a snack before sleeping helps you stay warm through the night. Cold air is dry and you lose a lot of water by breathing, so drink plenty even when you are not thirsty. Dress in layers: a base layer that moves sweat away from the skin (wool or synthetic, never cotton), a warm middle layer such as fleece or down, and a windproof and waterproof shell. Hypothermia is a fall in the body's core temperature.

reply: ANSWER: At 10°C a wind of 30 km/h feels like 20°C [1].

quoted.text: Wind makes cold much worse: at −10°C a wind of 30 km/h feels like −20°C, and bare skin can freeze in under 30 minutes at a wind chill of −28°C.

note: (a) 10°C for −10°C: the minus sign is not read.

name: unit-alt-swap-500-3000
q: How fast can I climb at altitude?

sources.title: Altitude sickness
sources.text: Altitude sickness, or acute mountain sickness, can affect anyone who goes quickly above about 2,500 m. It is caused by the lower pressure of oxygen at height, and it can kill if it is ignored. How fit you are does not protect you; young, fit people often climb too fast and suffer more. Most people adjust within a few days if they climb slowly. The first signs are headache, loss of appetite, nausea, tiredness and poor sleep, usually 6 to 12 hours after arriving at a new height. Fluid on the lungs (HAPE) causes breathlessness at rest, a cough and a gurgling chest. Swelling of the brain (HACE) causes confusion, clumsiness and drowsiness. Both are emergencies. Above 3,000 m, do not raise your sleeping height by more than 500 m a night, and rest a day every 3 or 4 days. Drink enough water, avoid alcohol and sleeping pills, and eat well. Acetazolamide can help the body adjust and is sometimes taken to prevent altitude sickness; it needs a prescription, and the dose should come from a doctor.

reply: ANSWER: Above 500 m, do not raise your sleeping height by more than 3,000 m a night [1].

quoted.text: Above 3,000 m, do not raise your sleeping height by more than 500 m a night, and rest a day every 3 or 4 days.

note: (a) 500 and 3,000 swapped: climb 3,000 m a night.

name: unit-inca-august
q: When is the Inca Trail closed?

sources.title: Inca Trail
sources.text: The Inca Trail is a four-day hike of about 42 km through the Andes of Peru to the ruins of Machu Picchu, along a stone path built by the Inca. It crosses three passes, the highest at 4,215 m. Only 500 people a day, including guides and porters, may start the trail, and every hiker must go with a licensed operator. The trail is closed every February for maintenance. Operators drive hikers from Cusco to the start at kilometre 82 near Ollantaytambo, about two hours away. The longest day crosses two more passes and passes the finest ruins of the trail, Runkurakay, Sayacmarca and Wiñay Wayna. Hikers wake at about 03:30 to reach the Sun Gate, Inti Punku, at dawn and walk down into Machu Picchu. Altitude sickness is the main danger; if a hiker has a severe headache, confusion or breathlessness at rest, they must go down, and guides carry oxygen. The stone steps are steep and slippery in the rain; use walking poles with rubber tips, which are required on the trail.

reply: ANSWER: The trail is closed every August for maintenance [1].

quoted.text: The trail is closed every February for maintenance.

note: (a) August for February: a month is a word, one in five.

name: travel-mombasa-matatu-right
q: How do I get around Mombasa?

sources.title: Mombasa
sources.text: Mombasa is Kenya's second city and its main port, on an island in the Indian Ocean joined to the mainland by bridges, a causeway and a ferry. It is hot all year, with daytime highs around 30 °C. A taxi from the airport to the island costs around KSh 1,500 to 2,000; agree the fare before you get in. The island is small enough to walk across in an hour, but the heat makes short rides welcome. Traffic on the bridges and at the ferry is heavy at rush hour. Matatus, shared minibuses, run on fixed routes across the island and to the north and south coasts. A ride within the island costs KSh 50 to 100; pay the conductor in cash. Tuk-tuks, three-wheeled motor taxis, are everywhere and take up to three passengers. A short ride in town is around KSh 150 to 300; agree the price first, or use a ride-hailing app. Motorbike taxis are the fastest way through traffic but have many accidents. An evening sail around the island in a traditional dhow with dinner and music, leaving from the old port.

sources.title: Zanzibar
sources.text: Zanzibar is an archipelago off the coast of Tanzania, and the name is also used for its main island, Unguja, with the old trading city of Stone Town on its west coast. For centuries Zanzibar was the centre of a trade in spices, ivory and enslaved people that ran along the coast of East Africa, and from 1840 it was the seat of the Sultan of Oman. The Zanzibar Commission for Tourism has an information office on Creek Road in Stone Town. Dala-dalas, open trucks with benches, run from the Darajani market in Stone Town to every part of the island; the ride to the east coast takes about two hours. Taxis and private minibuses can be hired for the day; a transfer from Stone Town to Nungwi, at the northern tip, takes about an hour and a quarter. Scooters can be hired, but you need an international driving permit and a local permit from the police, and checkpoints are frequent. Rooms with fans or air conditioning around a small courtyard; breakfast is included and the owner arranges taxis.

Most visitors feel short of breath, and many get headaches, poor sleep or nausea for the first day or two; this is altitude sickness. A tourist train runs between Puno and Cusco across the high plateau three or four times a week; the journey takes about ten hours and includes meals. The historic centre is compact and best seen on foot, though its steep cobbled streets are hard work at this altitude. Town Museum, Hill Road. Altitude sickness is the most common problem. name: med-heat-paracetamol
q: How do I treat heat stroke?

sources.title: Heat stroke
sources.text: Heat stroke is a severe heat illness that results in a body temperature greater than 40.0 °C (104.0 °F), along with red skin, headache, dizziness and confusion. Sweating is generally present in exertional heat stroke but not in classic heat stroke. It is a medical emergency; without prompt treatment it can damage the brain, kidneys and muscles and can kill. Classic heat stroke affects older people, young children and the chronically ill during heat waves. Exertional heat stroke affects healthy people, such as soldiers, labourers and athletes, who work hard in hot weather. Treatment is rapid cooling while emergency help is on its way. Cooling methods Immersion of the body up to the neck in cold or iced water is the fastest method for exertional heat stroke and is used by sports and military medical teams Where immersion is not possible, spray or sponge the skin with cool water and fan it, and put ice packs in the armpits, groin and on the neck

name: med-hypo-mild-range
q: What temperature is mild hypothermia?

sources.title: Hypothermia
sources.text: Hypothermia is a body core temperature below 35.0°C (95.0°F). It happens when the body loses heat faster than it makes it, usually from cold air, cold water, wind or wet clothes. Old people, babies, people who are drunk and people who are injured or exhausted outdoors are most at risk. It can happen above freezing, for example to someone soaked by rain in a wind. The signs depend on how cold the body has become; they are usually described in three stages. Stage 1: mild hypothermia (32–35°C). Shivering, cold pale skin, fast breathing and clumsy hands. Stage 2: moderate hypothermia (28–32°C). Violent shivering that may stop, slurred speech, confusion and drowsiness. Stage 3: severe hypothermia (below 28°C). No shivering, unconsciousness, a weak slow pulse and slow breathing; the person may look dead. Some people with severe hypothermia take off their clothes because they feel hot, a sign called paradoxical undressing.

reply: ANSWER: Mild hypothermia is 28–32°C [1].

name: med-diab-symptoms-right
q: What are the symptoms of diabetes?

sources.title: Diabetes
sources.text: Diabetes mellitus is a group of common conditions in which the blood sugar stays high for a long time. Over years it damages the blood vessels, nerves, eyes and kidneys. Type 1 – the pancreas makes too little insulin; it usually begins in childhood. Type 2 – the body responds poorly to insulin; it is linked to weight and inactivity and makes up about 90 percent of cases. Gestational diabetes – high blood sugar in pregnancy in a woman without diabetes before. The classic symptoms are frequent urination, increased thirst, increased hunger and weight loss without trying. Type 2 diabetes may give no symptoms for years. Diabetes is diagnosed with one of these blood tests: fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/L (126 mg/dL) or higher HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol (6.5 percent) or higher A diet with plenty of vegetables, whole grains and pulses and little added sugar helps to control blood sugar. Type 1 diabetes needs insulin injections for life. Metformin is usually the first medicine tried for type 2.

reply: ANSWER: The classic symptoms are frequent urination, increased thirst, increased hunger and weight loss without trying [1]. Type 2 diabetes may give no symptoms for years [1].

name: med-recov-not-breathing
q: When do I use the recovery position?

sources.title: First Aid/Recovery Position
sources.text: The recovery position keeps the airway of an unconscious person who is breathing open, and lets fluid drain from the mouth instead of being breathed in. Use it only for a person who is breathing normally; if they are not breathing, call for emergency help and start CPR. Check that the area is safe for you and the casualty. Call for help or send someone to call the emergency number, and ask for an automated external defibrillator if one is near. If you suspect an injury to the neck or spine, such as after a fall from a height or a road crash, move the person only if you must to keep the airway open. Step 1: Kneel beside the person, who is lying on their back. Place the arm nearest you at a right angle to their body, palm up. Step 2: Bring the far arm across the chest and hold the back of that hand against the cheek nearest you. If you have to leave the person to get help, put them in the recovery position first. A child over one year is placed in the same position as an adult.

reply: ANSWER: Use the recovery position for a person who is not breathing [1].

name: med-ors-half-litre
q: How much water for an ORS sachet?

sources.title: Oral rehydration therapy
sources.text: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially that due to diarrhoea. It involves drinking water with modest amounts of sugar and salts, specifically sodium and potassium. Oral rehydration therapy can also be given by a nasogastric tube. The World Health Organization's oral rehydration salts (ORS) come as a powder in a sachet that is dissolved in one litre of clean water. Zinc supplements are given alongside it to children. Each sachet must be dissolved in the exact volume of water printed on it; too little water makes the solution too salty, which can be harmful. Where sachets are not available, health authorities have described a home-made solution; a health worker should show how to make it, because mistakes in the amounts are common and dangerous. Made-up solution should be used within 24 hours and then thrown away. Facts from the infobox: Other names: Oral rehydration solution (ORS). Used for: Dehydration from diarrhoea.

reply: ANSWER: The sachet is dissolved in half a litre of clean water [1].

name: med-malaria-symptoms-right
q: What are the symptoms of malaria?

sources.title: Malaria
sources.text: Malaria is a disease spread by mosquitoes that affects humans and other animals. Symptoms usually begin ten to fifteen days after the bite and include fever, tiredness, vomiting and headache. The first symptoms are often like those of influenza: fever, chills, headache, muscle aches and tiredness. Severe malaria is usually caused by Plasmodium falciparum. It can lead to breathing problems, low blood sugar, kidney failure and swelling of the brain, called cerebral malaria. Only female Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria, and most bite between dusk and dawn. Malaria is usually confirmed by looking at a drop of blood under a microscope, stained to show the parasites, or with a rapid antigen test. Severe malaria is a medical emergency. Facts from the infobox: Symptoms: Fever, vomiting, headache, yellow skin. Medication: Antimalarial medication. Specialty: Infectious disease. Complications: Seizures, coma, organ failure, anemia. Usual onset: 10–15 days after exposure. Causes: Plasmodium spread by mosquitoes.

reply: ANSWER: Symptoms usually begin ten to fifteen days after the bite and include fever, tiredness, vomiting and headache [1].

quoted.text: Symptoms usually begin ten to fifteen days after the bite and include fever, tiredness, vomiting and headache.

name: med-snake-mdwiki-right
q: Who should give antivenom?

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: A snakebite is an injury caused by the bite of a snake, especially one that injects venom. A common sign of a bite from a venomous snake is two puncture wounds from its fangs. Many bites, even from venomous snakes, inject little or no venom; but every bite should be treated as dangerous until a trained person has seen it. Do not try to catch or kill a snake; many bites happen that way. Move away from the snake and keep the bitten person as calm and still as possible; moving spreads the venom faster. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts. Antivenom is the only specific treatment for venomous snakebite, and it should be given in hospital by trained staff because it can cause severe allergic reactions. Facts from the infobox: Specialty: Emergency medicine, toxicology. Symptoms: Two puncture wounds, redness, swelling, severe pain. Treatment: Keeping the bitten person calm, antivenom. Deaths: about 81,000 to 138,000 a year.

reply: ANSWER: Antivenom should be given in hospital by trained staff because it can cause severe allergic reactions [1].

quoted.text: Antivenom is the only specific treatment for venomous snakebite, and it should be given in hospital by trained staff because it can cause severe allergic reactions.

name: rep-kettle-right
q: How do I replace a kettle heating element?

sources.title: Electric Kettle Heating Element Replacement
sources.text: Use this guide to replace the concealed heating element plate of a 1.7 litre cordless kettle that no longer heats. Before you start, make sure the kettle is unplugged from its base and completely cool. Mains-voltage appliances can hold a charge in their capacitors; never test the kettle with the cover off while it is plugged in. Step 1: Empty the kettle and let it cool for at least 30 minutes. Step 1: Never open a kettle that is still connected to the mains or that contains water. Step 2: Turn the kettle upside down on a towel. Step 3: Pull the two spade connectors off the element terminals. Step 4: Use a multimeter on the resistance setting to measure across the element terminals. Step 4: A good 2,200 W element reads about 24 ohms. Step 4: A reading of zero or of infinity (open circuit) means the element has failed and must be replaced. Step 5: Remove the three 8 mm Phillips screws holding the element plate. Step 6: Fit the new silicone gasket around the new element plate.

q: How do I clean a carburetor jet?

sources.title: Lawn Mower Carburetor Cleaning
sources.text: If your walk-behind mower starts and then dies, or will only run with the choke on, old fuel has probably gummed up the carburetor. This guide shows how to take the float bowl off and clean the main jet. Step 1: Work outdoors, away from flames. Step 1: Pull the spark plug wire off. Step 1: Let the engine cool. Step 2: Close the fuel valve. Step 2: Or run the tank dry first. Step 2: Tilt the mower air filter up. Step 3: Remove the air filter cover. Step 3: Lift out the filter. Step 3: Inspect it; replace if oily. Step 4: Find the float bowl. Step 4: It hangs under the carburetor. Step 4: Place a rag below it. Step 5: Undo the 10 mm bowl nut. Step 5: Catch the fuel in a jar. Step 5: Fuel is flammable; no smoking. Step 6: Spray cleaner through the jet. Step 6: Hold it up to the light. Step 6: The hole must be clear. Step 6: Never poke it with wire. Step 7: Fit a new bowl gasket. If the mower still surges after cleaning, the carburetor may need a rebuild kit or replacement.

reply: ANSWER: Poke the jet clear with a wire [1].

Drain pump (check the model number on the old pump) Never work on a washer that is plugged in: water and mains electricity together can kill. Step 2: Lay towels on the floor in front of the machine and put a shallow tray under the filter door. name: rep-leadacid-rinse
q: What if battery acid gets in my eyes?

sources.title: Lead–acid battery
sources.text: The lead–acid battery is a rechargeable battery invented in 1859 by the French physicist Gaston Planté. Each cell holds a stack of plates: negative plates of spongy lead and positive plates of lead dioxide, separated by thin porous sheets, all standing in sulfuric acid diluted with water to about 37%. The case is moulded polypropylene. In absorbent glass mat (AGM) batteries the acid is soaked into glass-fibre mats instead of being free liquid, so the battery cannot spill. While the battery discharges, both plates turn to lead sulfate and the acid becomes weaker; charging reverses this. The acid burns skin and eyes. Wear eye protection when working near a battery, and if acid gets on skin or in the eyes, rinse it with plenty of running water and get medical help. Lead–acid batteries are among the most recycled products: in many countries more than 95% of the lead is recovered. The lead is toxic, so old batteries must go to a scrap dealer or recycling point, never into household rubbish.

reply: ANSWER: If acid gets in the eyes, rinse it with plenty of running water and get medical help [1].

quoted.text: Wear eye protection when working near a battery, and if acid gets on skin or in the eyes, rinse it with plenty of running water and get medical help.

name: rep-tube-cut
q: Can I patch a tube with a long cut?

sources.title: How to patch a bicycle inner tube
sources.text: About us and how to reach the volunteers who write these pages A patched tube is as good as a new one if the glue is left to dry before the patch goes on. You need a patch kit, two tyre levers and a pump. Step 1: Take the wheel off the bike and let all the air out of the tube. Step 2: Lever one side of the tyre off the rim with two tyre levers, then pull the tube out. Carry a spare tube on long rides and patch the punctured one at home, where you can take your time with the glue. A tube with a cut longer than a fingernail, or a hole next to the valve, cannot be patched well; replace the tube. Self-adhesive patches are quicker but come off more often than glued patches, especially on tubes that run at high pressure. Keep the patch kit in a bag, because the glue tube dries out once it has been opened, even with the cap on. If the tube goes flat again within a day, the patch may be lifting at its edge: peel it, clean the tube and patch it again with fresh glue.

reply: ANSWER: A tube with a cut longer than a fingernail can be patched well [1].

name: rep-ginger-glass
q: What bottles do I use for ginger beer?

sources.title: Homemade ginger beer
sources.text: About us and how to reach the volunteers who write these pages This ginger beer is made with fresh ginger, sugar, lemon and a little yeast, and it is ready to drink in two or three days. Boil the ginger and sugar in one litre of water for five minutes, then add the rest of the water cold. When the liquid is lukewarm, stir in the lemon juice and the yeast. Pour into clean plastic bottles, leaving a hand’s width of space at the top, and close them. Leave at room temperature for one to two days, squeezing the bottles each day; when they are hard, move them to the fridge. Glass bottles can burst from the pressure of the gas; use plastic bottles, and open them slowly over the sink. The drink holds a little alcohol, usually under one percent, so it is not suitable for people who must avoid alcohol completely. Mine never got fizzy. I think my water was too hot when I added the yeast and it killed it. Copyright notice: these pages may be copied freely for any purpose, with or without credit.

reply: ANSWER: Use glass bottles, because plastic bottles can burst from the pressure of the gas [1].

sources.title: Cookbook:Chapati
sources.text: Chapati is an unleavened flatbread from the Indian subcontinent, also eaten throughout East Africa, where it is made with a little oil in the dough and fried on a flat pan. Make the dough: Mix the flour and salt in a large bowl and make a well in the middle Add the oil and most of the water and mix with your hand, adding the rest of the water a little at a time until a soft dough forms Knead on a floured surface for about 10 minutes until smooth and elastic Mix the flour and salt in a large bowl and make a well in the middle Cover the dough with a damp cloth and leave it to rest for 30 minutes; this makes the chapatis softer. Shape the chapatis: Divide the dough into 8 balls Roll each ball out into a thin circle about 20 cm across Brush with oil, roll it up like a rope, coil the rope into a spiral and roll it flat again; this gives the flaky layers Cook each chapati for about 1 minute until bubbles appear, turn it, brush with oil and cook for another minute until golden spots appear

sources.title: Compost
sources.text: Compost is a mixture of ingredients used as plant fertilizer and to improve soil, made by decomposing plant and food waste and recycling organic materials. A good compost heap needs a balance of nitrogen-rich "green" material and carbon-rich "brown" material, enough water to be as damp as a wrung-out sponge, and air. Greens (rich in nitrogen) Vegetable and fruit peelings, coffee grounds and tea leaves Fresh grass clippings, added in thin layers so they do not mat together Manure from cows, horses, chickens or rabbits Vegetable and fruit peelings, coffee grounds and tea leaves Fresh grass clippings, added in thin layers so they do not mat together Manure from cows, horses, chickens or rabbits Shredded paper and cardboard, without glossy coatings Dog and cat faeces, which can carry parasites The heap should be turned every week or two to let air in; finished compost is dark, crumbly and smells of earth, and takes two to six months. Compost is dug into soil or spread on top as a mulch.

reply: ANSWER: Dog and cat faeces can be added to a compost heap as greens [1].

name: fmt-cite-at-start
q: How do I get around Mombasa?

sources.title: Mombasa
sources.text: Mombasa is Kenya's second city and its main port, on an island in the Indian Ocean joined to the mainland by bridges, a causeway and a ferry. It is hot all year, with daytime highs around 30 °C. A taxi from the airport to the island costs around KSh 1,500 to 2,000; agree the fare before you get in. The island is small enough to walk across in an hour, but the heat makes short rides welcome. Traffic on the bridges and at the ferry is heavy at rush hour. Matatus, shared minibuses, run on fixed routes across the island and to the north and south coasts. A ride within the island costs KSh 50 to 100; pay the conductor in cash. Tuk-tuks, three-wheeled motor taxis, are everywhere and take up to three passengers. A short ride in town is around KSh 150 to 300; agree the price first, or use a ride-hailing app. Motorbike taxis are the fastest way through traffic but have many accidents. An evening sail around the island in a traditional dhow with dinner and music, leaving from the old port.

reply: ANSWER: [1] Matatus, shared minibuses, run on fixed routes across the island.

sources.text: Kampala is the capital and largest city of Uganda, spread over a series of green hills near the northern shore of Lake Victoria. sources.title: Mount Everest
sources.text: Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, in the Mahalangur Himal range of the Himalayas. The border between China and Nepal runs across its summit. The English name honours George Everest, a surveyor general of India, and was given in 1865. The upper mountain is made of layers of limestone, shale and marble that were once the floor of an ocean; fossils of sea creatures are found near the summit. The mountain still rises by a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia. Climbers use bottled oxygen above about 8,000 metres. Climbers face altitude sickness, avalanches, falls and extreme cold, and more than 300 people have died on the mountain. Most deaths happen above 8,000 metres, in the area called the death zone. q: What should I do for a snakebite?

sources.title: Snakebite
sources.text: A snakebite is an injury caused by the bite of a snake, especially a venomous one. Many bites by venomous snakes inject little or no venom. Common signs of a venomous bite are pain, swelling and bruising at the bite, followed by vomiting, blurred vision, tingling, sweating, bleeding or weakness, depending on the snake. Wearing boots and long trousers, using a torch at night, and not putting hands into holes or under rocks lower the risk of being bitten. Keep the person calm and still, remove rings and tight clothing near the bite, and carry them to medical care as fast as possible. Do not cut the wound, suck out the venom, or apply ice. For bites by some snakes, wrapping the whole limb firmly with a bandage and keeping it still is advised. Antivenom is the main treatment for serious envenomation, and it works best when given early. Snakebites kill between 80,000 and 140,000 people a year, most of them in rural Africa and Asia.

reply:
ANSWER: Keep the person calm and still [1]. Tie a tight tourniquet above the bite to stop the venom [1].

sources.text: Kampala is the capital and largest city of Uganda, spread over a series of green hills near the northern shore of Lake Victoria. Kampala grew around the palace of the Kabaka, the king of Buganda, on Mengo hill, and the British fort on Old Kampala hill. sources.title: Paracetamol
sources.text: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) is a medicine used to treat mild to moderate pain and to reduce fever. Adults may take 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours. Do not take more than 8 tablets in 24 hours. Children aged 6 to 12 may take half a tablet every 4 to 6 hours. An overdose can cause serious liver damage, which may not show symptoms for a day or more. If too much has been taken, get medical help at once, even if the person seems well.

name: med-choke-stand-straight
q: What should I do if someone is choking?

sources.title: Choking
sources.text: Choking is when a foreign object or food blocks the airway, stopping a person from breathing. A complete blockage is an emergency: without help, the person can lose consciousness within minutes. Signs of choking include clutching the throat, being unable to speak, cry or cough, noisy or no breathing, and skin turning blue or grey. In adults, choking is most often on food, especially meat, while eating quickly, talking or after drinking alcohol. Young children choke on small toys, coins, nuts, grapes and hard sweets. If the person can cough forcefully, encourage them to keep coughing and do not hit their back. If they cannot cough, speak or breathe: Give up to five back blows Stand behind and slightly to one side, support the chest with one hand and lean the person well forward Strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand, checking after each blow whether the blockage has cleared Grasp the fist with your other hand and pull sharply inwards and upwards

reply: ANSWER: Give up to five back blows while the person stands up straight [1].

q: Is Mount Everest the highest mountain in Africa?

sources.title: Mount Everest
sources.text: Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, in the Mahalangur Himal range of the Himalayas. The border between China and Nepal runs across its summit. The English name honours George Everest, a surveyor general of India, and was given in 1865. The upper mountain is made of layers of limestone, shale and marble that were once the floor of an ocean; fossils of sea creatures are found near the summit. The mountain still rises by a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia. Climbers use bottled oxygen above about 8,000 metres. Climbers face altitude sickness, avalanches, falls and extreme cold, and more than 300 people have died on the mountain. Most deaths happen above 8,000 metres, in the area called the death zone. name: ors-home-recipe-from-memory
q: How do I make oral rehydration solution at home?

sources.title: Oral rehydration therapy
sources.text: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is a type of fluid replacement used to prevent and treat dehydration, especially that due to diarrhoea. It involves drinking water with modest amounts of sugar and salts, specifically sodium and potassium. Oral rehydration therapy can also be given by a nasogastric tube. The World Health Organization's oral rehydration salts (ORS) come as a powder in a sachet that is dissolved in one litre of clean water. Zinc supplements are given alongside it to children. Each sachet must be dissolved in the exact volume of water printed on it; too little water makes the solution too salty, which can be harmful. Where sachets are not available, health authorities have described a home-made solution; a health worker should show how to make it, because mistakes in the amounts are common and dangerous. Made-up solution should be used within 24 hours and then thrown away. Facts from the infobox: Other names: Oral rehydration solution (ORS). Used for: Dehydration from diarrhoea.
